answer: First‑token latency is the time until the model produces its first output token, reflecting the initial inference cost and any warm‑up. Total latency sums the time to generate the entire sequence, including the incremental decoding cost of each subsequent token.

First‑token latency measures only the time until the model emits its first token, reflecting the initial inference and any warm‑up delay. Total latency accumulates the time for all subsequent decoding steps, so it depends on output length and per‑token cost.

First‑token latency measures the time from request to the very first output token, capturing the model’s warm‑up and initial inference cost. Total latency sums the time to produce all tokens, reflecting repeated decoding steps that can reuse earlier computations, so it generally grows with sequence length.

Scaled dot‑product attention computes the attention weights by first taking the dot product of each query vector with all key vectors, scaling the resulting scores by the inverse square root of the key dimension \(d_k\), and then applying a softmax.  
Mathematically, for query matrix \(Q\), key matrix \(K\), and value matrix \(V\),

\[
\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V .
\]

The softmax outputs a probability distribution over the keys, which serves as the weights for the weighted sum of the values [E1][E2].

The Transformer uses multi‑head attention because it lets the model attend to information from several different representation subspaces simultaneously. With a single attention head the weighted sum of the values tends to average out distinct patterns, limiting the model’s ability to capture diverse relationships in the data. Multi‑head attention therefore enables the network to jointly focus on multiple aspects of the input at each position, improving expressiveness and performance. Empirically, the authors found that a single‑head variant performed noticeably worse (≈0.9 BLEU points lower) than the eight‑head baseline, confirming the benefit of multiple heads [E3, E2].

The Transformer has no recurrence or convolution, so it cannot automatically capture the order of tokens.  
To give the model access to positional information, the authors add **positional encodings** to the token embeddings at the bottom of both the encoder and decoder stacks.  
These encodings have the same dimensionality as the embeddings (dmodel) so they can be summed with the embeddings.  
The paper uses sinusoidal functions of different frequencies:

\[
\text{PE}(pos,2i)=\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right),\qquad
\text{PE}(pos,2i+1)=\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)
\]

The choice of sine/cosine allows the model to learn relative positions easily, because for any fixed offset \(k\), \(\text{PE}_{pos+k}\) can be expressed as a linear function of \(\text{PE}_{pos}\).  
The authors also tried learned positional embeddings and found similar performance, but chose the sinusoidal form because it may enable extrapolation to longer sequences than seen during training.  

Thus, positional encoding injects absolute/relative positional information into the model, enabling it to use the order of tokens despite lacking recurrence or convolution.

The encoder stack consists of six identical layers, each with two sub‑layers: a multi‑head self‑attention mechanism followed by a position‑wise fully‑connected feed‑forward network. Each sub‑layer is wrapped in a residual connection and layer‑normalised, and all sub‑layers output vectors of dimension \(d_{\text{model}}=512\) [E1].

The decoder stack also has six identical layers, but each layer contains **three** sub‑layers. In addition to the masked multi‑head self‑attention and the feed‑forward network, it includes a third sub‑layer that performs multi‑head attention over the encoder’s output (encoder‑decoder attention). The decoder’s self‑attention is masked so that a position can attend only to earlier positions, preserving the auto‑regressive property, and the output embeddings are offset by one position to enforce this masking [E1][E5].

The Inner Monologue component is designed to let Moshi generate a time‑aligned text representation of its own speech and use that text as a prefix to the audio tokens it produces. This scaffolding improves the linguistic quality of the generated speech and gives the model a hierarchical, per‑frame generation structure that does not lengthen the Transformer sequence. It also enables Moshi to support streaming speech‑to‑speech, TTS, and ASR by combining text and acoustic tokens in a single generative model. The authors note that Inner Monologue has one of the most critical impacts on speech quality and allows the system to produce arbitrary voices and conditions without explicit speaker‑turn segmentation. [E1][E4][E5]

Moshi adopts a hierarchical autoregressive design so that it can generate speech in a coarse‑to‑fine, streaming manner.  
The model first predicts high‑level semantic tokens and then refines them into acoustic tokens, a strategy that the authors show is essential for producing intelligible, consistent speech.  By extending the hierarchy to include text tokens as a per‑time‑step prefix, Moshi can also generate text alongside audio, enabling streaming ASR and TTS from the same model.  This hierarchical approach lets Moshi integrate semantic and acoustic tokens into a single generative model—unlike prior work that uses separate stages—thereby improving audio quality and length while remaining real‑time capable.

Dynamic Chunking (DC) decides where to place a boundary by learning a **routing module** that is trained jointly with the rest of the network.  
* The routing module predicts a binary boundary indicator for each token position, and the downstream down‑sampler keeps only the vectors at the predicted boundaries, thereby compressing the sequence while preserving semantically important positions.  
* The decision is **content‑ and context‑aware**: during training the model learns to place boundaries at natural semantic units such as whitespace, but it also merges or splits words depending on the surrounding content (e.g., it may merge multiple words or split a word into sub‑chunks when the characters are highly predictable).  
* A **ratio loss** hyper‑parameter controls the target chunk size, encouraging the routing module to produce a desired average number of tokens per chunk.  
* Because the routing module is optimized end‑to‑end, the boundaries emerge from gradient signals rather than from fixed heuristics.  

Thus, dynamic chunking creates a boundary when the routing module’s learned decision, guided by the ratio loss and the data’s semantic structure, indicates that a new chunk should start.

The Transformer was trained with the **Adam optimizer** (β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.98, ε = 10⁻⁹) and a **learning‑rate schedule** that linearly increases the rate for the first 4 000 training steps (warm‑up) and then decreases it proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. This schedule is defined by  

\[
\text{lrate} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5}\;\min\!\big(step_{\text{num}}^{-0.5},\; step_{\text{num}}\;warmup_{\text{steps}}^{-1.5}\big)
\]

with \(warmup_{\text{steps}} = 4000\).  

[E4]

The Transformer blocks future tokens from influencing a decoder position by applying a **causal mask** to the self‑attention score matrix.  
During scaled‑dot‑product attention, all entries that would allow a query at position *i* to attend to any position *j > i* are set to \(-\infty\) before the softmax. This forces the softmax to assign zero probability to those illegal connections, so each decoder step can only attend to itself and earlier positions. The mask is applied together with the usual offset of the output embeddings, ensuring that the prediction for position *i* depends only on known outputs at positions \< *i*.[E1][E3]

The Helium text language model serves as the linguistic backbone of Moshi.  Moshi is built on top of Helium, using its pre‑trained text‑only knowledge to generate the time‑aligned text tokens that precede the acoustic tokens.  This “inner monologue” of text tokens improves the linguistic quality of the generated speech and provides the foundation for Moshi’s full‑duplex dialogue capabilities.  [E4][E5]

Moshi tokenizes audio with a dedicated neural audio codec called **Mimi**. Mimi learns a compact representation of speech by **combining semantic and acoustic information into a single tokenizer**. The tokenizer is built with **residual vector quantization** and is further refined through **knowledge distillation** from a self‑supervised speech model. The resulting tokens are then used as one of the streams in Moshi’s multi‑stream architecture, where the model jointly predicts text tokens and audio tokens for both the user and Moshi itself.  

[ E2 ]

The Moshi paper reports several safety analyses:

1. **Toxicity analysis** – The authors evaluate the text generated by Moshi on the ALERT benchmark, which measures safety across categories such as hate, self‑harm, weapon, crime, sex, and substance. They present category‑wise safety scores and an overall safety score for Moshi compared with other large language models. [E1][E3]  
2. **Safety‑related questions** – In the Safety section the paper outlines four specific safety concerns that are investigated:  
   * Production of toxic content.  
   * Avoiding regurgitation of audio content from the training set.  
   * Ensuring the model uses the intended voice.  
   * Identifying whether a given content was generated by Moshi. [E2]

The H‑Net routing module detects chunk boundaries by predicting a boundary indicator for each pair of adjacent elements. It does this through a similarity score computed between neighboring tokens, which the module uses to decide where to place a boundary. [E1]

Boundary probabilities are derived from the cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs.  
For each position \(t\) the encoder output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t\) is projected to query and key vectors:

\[
\mathbf{q}_t = \mathbf{W}_q \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t,\qquad
\mathbf{k}_t = \mathbf{W}_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t .
\]

The boundary probability \(p_t\) is then

\[
p_t = \frac12\!\left(1-\frac{\mathbf{q}_t^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{t-1}}
{\|\mathbf{q}_t\|\;\|\mathbf{k}_{t-1}\|}\right)\in[0,1] ,
\]

with \(p_1 = 1.0\) by definition to start the sequence with a boundary.  
This formulation scales the cosine similarity of adjacent representations into a probability that is high when the two vectors are dissimilar (indicating a boundary) and low when they are similar. [E1]
The boundary indicator is set to 1 when the boundary probability is at least 0.5, i.e., the threshold used is 0.5. [E2]

The downsampler compresses the encoder outputs by **selecting only the vectors that are marked as boundaries**.  
For each time step \(t\) it checks the boundary indicator \(b_t\):  

* If \(b_t = 1\), the corresponding encoder vector \(\hat{x}_t\) is kept in the compressed sequence \(x_{s+1}\).  
* If \(b_t = 0\), that vector is discarded.  

The same selection rule is applied to the boundary probabilities, compressing \(p_s\) into \(P_{s+1}\) for use in the dechunking layer.  

[ E1 ] [ E2 ]

The ratio loss is introduced to regularize the dynamic chunking process so that the model does not collapse to trivial extremes—either keeping almost all vectors (losing computational savings) or compressing too aggressively (losing important information).  Inspired by load‑balancing in Mixture‑of‑Experts, the loss encourages the network to match a target compression ratio by providing continuous feedback through the average boundary probability, thereby guiding the model toward the desired ratio in practice. [E2]
